metadata.title: Predictors of students’ global competence in China, Germany, Turkey, and Mexico: A cross-cultural comparative study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for the global competence framework, drawing on both a cognitive test component and student questionnaire items, but it does not report applying any PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the analysis section. The authors describe PISA’s two-stage probability proportional to size school sampling and random student selection within schools, implying a complex survey design, yet no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is named and no BRR/jackknife method is reported. Because the analysis is conducted with multilevel modeling (HLM) rather than ML algorithms, the manuscript does not provide a weighting strategy for producing population-representative estimates. The analytic sample is restricted to the 27 economies that participated in both the global competence test and module, and further restricted to the four selected cultural-context countries/economies (China via Hong Kong SAR, Germany, Turkey, Mexico).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are four questionnaire-based global competence scales (self-efficacy, respect, awareness, global mindedness) rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores, so plausible values are not applicable to the modeled outcomes. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., complete-case exclusion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because questionnaire items typically have nonresponse. As a result, the robustness of the estimates to missingness cannot be evaluated from the provided methods.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 global competence data restricted to economies that participated in both the global competence test and the global competence module; then selected four countries/economies based on World Values Survey (WVS 7th) cultural map quadrants: China operationalized as Hong Kong SAR (mainland not participating), Germany, Turkey, and Mexico. The sample includes students in grades 7–12 nested within schools, with total N=25,677 students across 771 schools (China/Hong Kong SAR: 6037 in 113 schools; Germany: 5451 in 188 schools; Turkey: 6890 in 186 schools; Mexico: 7299 in 284 schools). No additional item-level inclusion/exclusion rules or missing-response criteria are reported.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — self-efficacy regarding global issues scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel HLM coefficients (β) with standard errors; no predictive ML metrics (e.g., Accuracy/AUC/R²) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Global Competence the study leveraged cultural possessions (CULTPOS), perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), perception of co-operation (PERCOOP), and gender to predict self-efficacy regarding global issues, finding that CULTPOS, COMPICT, and PERCOOP were positive and statistically significant predictors across countries (β ranges: CULTPOS 0.079–0.151; COMPICT 0.067–0.155; PERCOOP 0.072–0.087). Gender effects differed by country (e.g., Germany: β=-0.139; Turkey: β=0.091; Mexico: β=0.056), and exchange programmes were significant for self-efficacy in Germany (β=0.257) and Mexico (β=0.097). This indicates that strengthening students’ cultural capital, ICT competence, and cooperative school climate may raise students’ confidence in handling global issues, though the study is cross-sectional and does not provide causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — respect for people from other cultural backgrounds scale
main_findings.target_variable: Respect for people from other cultural backgrounds
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel HLM coefficients (β) with standard errors; no predictive ML metrics reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Global Competence the study leveraged gender, cultural possessions (CULTPOS), perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), and perception of co-operation (PERCOOP) to predict respect for people from other cultural backgrounds, finding that gender was significantly associated with respect in all four countries (girls higher; β ranges -0.378 to -0.233). It also found that COMPICT and PERCOOP were negative and statistically significant predictors of respect across countries (COMPICT β=-0.203 to -0.074; PERCOOP β=-0.198 to -0.093), while CULTPOS was negative and significant in China, Germany, and Turkey (β=-0.087 to -0.049). This indicates that the relationship between digital/learning resources and respect may be context-dependent and not uniformly positive, implying that policy should pair ICT and cooperation initiatives with explicit intercultural respect curricula rather than assuming direct benefits.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — awareness of intercultural communication scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel HLM coefficients (β) with standard errors; no predictive ML metrics reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Global Competence the study leveraged gender, cultural possessions (CULTPOS), perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), and perception of co-operation (PERCOOP) to predict awareness of intercultural communication, finding that all four student-level predictors were positively and significantly associated with awareness in all countries (gender β=0.076–0.203; CULTPOS β=0.039–0.058; COMPICT β=0.117–0.144; PERCOOP β=0.100–0.160). At the school level, exchange programmes were significant for awareness in Germany (β=0.246) and Mexico (β=0.091), and foreign languages in curriculum were significant in Germany (β=0.270). This indicates that combining student cultural capital and ICT competence with school-level internationalization and language curriculum support may improve students’ intercultural communication awareness, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Global Competence (grades 7–12) — global mindedness scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel HLM coefficients (β) with standard errors; no predictive ML metrics reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Global Competence the study leveraged gender, cultural possessions (CULTPOS), perception of co-operation (PERCOOP), perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), and exchange programmes (EXCHPG) to predict global mindedness, finding that gender was significantly positive in Germany, Turkey, and Mexico (β=0.089–0.113) and not significant in China. It also found positive and significant effects of CULTPOS and PERCOOP across countries (CULTPOS β=0.033–0.135; PERCOOP β=0.120–0.184), and positive effects of COMPICT in China, Turkey, and Mexico (β=0.082–0.113), while COMPICT was not significant in Germany (β=-0.018). This indicates that policies promoting cultural capital, cooperative school practices, and ICT competence—along with exchange opportunities—may enhance students’ sense of responsibility for collective well-being, but effects vary by national context.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-cultural comparative study uses PISA 2018 global competence data (grades 7–12) from four economies: China operationalized via Hong Kong SAR (n=6037), Germany (n=5451), Turkey (n=6890), and Mexico (n=7299), totaling 25,677 students nested in 771 schools. The authors model four questionnaire-based global competence dimensions—self-efficacy, respect, awareness of intercultural communication, and global mindedness—using multilevel HLM (two-level student/school structure), not PV-based achievement. Across countries, cultural possessions (CULTPOS), perceived ICT competence (COMPICT), and perception of co-operation (PERCOOP) show consistent positive associations with self-efficacy and awareness, while their relationships with respect are negative and context-dependent. The paper reports multilevel regression coefficients (β) and standard errors but no predictive ML metrics (e.g., Accuracy/AUC/R²). Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling and no causal identification, so findings should be interpreted as correlational patterns rather than effects of interventions.
